title: Tycoon Originally Meant the Shogun
hook: The English word “tycoon” for a business magnate comes from the Japanese taikun, which was first a title of the shogun
summary: Tycoon comes from the Japanese taikun. It first referred to the shogun, and the sense of a powerful businessman came after World War 1.

text: A lithograph shows Perry's party landing to meet the Japanese representatives.
The shogun's formal title is seii taishogun, which means something close to military commander.
So for diplomatic documents, a Japanese encyclopedia explains, a separate title was used: taikun.
At first, Westerners translated this as something like emperor or majestic ruler.
Later, a word that copied the sound of taikun took hold. In English, it is “tycoon.”
English dictionaries record the first use of “tycoon” in 1857, with the meaning shogun.
In 1861, the word was applied to Lincoln.
It spread to mean an important person, and only after World War 1 did it come to mean a rich, powerful businessman.
